The Thick-billed murre (Uria lomvia) is a pursuit-diving alcid that exhibits a single-egg clutch, with females laying exactly one egg per nesting attempt [N_R_i = one egg per nesting attempt]. On the cliffs of the Arctic, breeding pairs typically manage only a single successful brood each year [F_R_i = single successful brood each year], a constraint imposed by the brief polar summer. Under the thermal conditions characteristic of an active adult bird (40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]), the developing chick hatches after an incubation period of approximately 33 days [ab = approximately 33 days], though this duration is measured at the egg's typical incubation temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. At the moment of hatching, the wet weight of the neonate is about 70.4 grams [Wwb = about 70.4 grams], a modest mass that reflects the considerable yolk reserves already consumed during embryonic development. This initial size stands in stark contrast to the ultimate size the bird will attain as a fully grown adult, which is among the largest of the alcids, a direct consequence of its energy-intensive foraging strategy.

Once the chick emerges, it enters a rapid growth phase on the open cliff ledge, a precarious environment where it remains for roughly 21 days [tx = roughly 21 days] before taking its first flight, a milestone achieved while its parents maintain a body temperature near 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. During this nestling period, which typically spans 18 to 25 days on the cliff, the semi-precocial chick is fed continuously by both parents, accumulating mass at a remarkable rate. The maximum adult body mass recorded for this species is 964 grams [Wwi = 964 grams], a value that places the Thick-billed murre among the heavier alcids, a trait that correlates with its deep-diving capabilities in cold Arctic waters. This ultimate wet weight is attained after the juvenile has completed its post-fledging growth and has begun to forage independently at sea.

Sexual maturation in the Thick-billed murre is not a rapid process; the onset of puberty occurs at approximately 63 days after the chick leaves the nest [tp = approximately 63 days after the chick leaves the nest], again under the elevated metabolic conditions of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. This timing is notably late for an alcid of this size, as physiological development is heavily focused on achieving the necessary body condition and flight capability required for survival in the demanding marine environment. The time to the first successful reproductive event, or the age at first brood, is considerably more protracted. Field studies have documented that individuals do not typically return to the natal colony and attempt to breed until 1862 days after their own hatching [tR = 1862 days after their own hatching], a delay that allows for extensive learning of foraging routes and social structures at the colony at a temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C].

In terms of overall longevity, the Thick-billed murre is a remarkably long-lived seabird. In the thermal context of routine activity at 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C], the maximum documented lifespan for the species reaches approximately 29 years [am = approximately 29 years], a duration that is typical for a pelagic bird with a 'slow' life-history strategy. Such a long life is made possible by the low annual reproductive output, with that single egg [Ri = annual reproductive output, with that single egg] and single brood per year [F_R_i = single brood per year] per year acting as a trade-off for high adult survivorship. Adults face significant energetic demands to sustain such an extended lifespan.

This reproductive strategy is tightly linked to the harshness of the Arctic environment, where the brief ice-free season compresses the entire breeding cycle. The extended pre-breeding period allows young birds to develop critical foraging proficiency before committing to the immense energetic costs of reproduction. The species has evolved a life-history pattern that emphasizes adult survival at the expense of annual fecundity, a common adaptation among pelagic seabirds facing unpredictable food resources and extreme climatic conditions. Population modeling for Thick-billed murres suggests that even small increases in adult mortality can lead to rapid population declines, underscoring the importance of protecting mature individuals from anthropogenic threats such as oil spills and bycatch in fisheries.
